title.en: An Act of Kindness: The Red Cloth, the Stones, and the Canes
title.zh: 一樁善行：紅布、飛石與魔杖

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness', eBook #8299

summary.en: Andres ransoms a small snake with his five cents for rice; at the snake-cave the chief gives him a red cloth that supplies whatever he wants. He trades it to a hut-woman for two fighting stones, then sends the stones back to seize it again, dining at a witch's hut and accepting two canes that kill on command. When a selfish rich neighbor sends robbers to his cottage, the stones and canes leave every thief dead.
summary.zh: 安德烈斯以買米的五仙贖下一條小蛇；蛇王贈他『要什麼有什麼』的紅布。他以紅布換得兩枚會打人的飛石，又遣石索回紅布；在巫婆小屋飽餐後再得兩根能誅敵的魔杖。當自私的富鄰遣盜夜襲時，飛石與魔杖盡誅群盜。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Knapsack-Hat-and-Horn cycle with a unique pair of fighting stones, which Fansler calls 'very primitive.'

passages.text: Early one morning Andres went out to buy five cents' worth of rice. On his way he came across a man who was about to kill a small snake. 'Please don't kill the poor creature! Did it harm you?' 'No, but it may bite us or some other passer-by,' answered the man, again drawing out his bolo; but Andres restrained him: 'Leave it alone, for pity's sake! Here are five cents! Don't injure the harmless creature!' The man, very glad to get the money, went away; and the snake said to Andres, 'Kind friend, come home with me. There you will find our huge chief snake, and many others like myself... When we reach our dwelling, I will recommend you to our chief. He will be harsh to you at first, since you are a stranger; but never mind that! When he asks you what you want, ask him to give you his red cloth. This enchanted cloth can supply you with whatever you want.' So the two friends started for the horrible snake-cave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Who is that stranger with you — a murderer, or a robber?' hissed the chief as soon as the snake and Andres entered. 'He is neither of the two. Had it not been for him, my life would have been lost.' 'Well, what reward do you want me to give you?' 'Only your red cloth, and nothing else,' answered Andres. The chief went into a very dark cell and got out the red cloth: 'Since you have saved the life of one of our number, I give you this cloth as a reward. You can ask of it anything you want.' It was now ten o'clock, and Andres had not yet bought rice for breakfast: 'Poor mother! she must be very hungry' — and he asked the red cloth to bring him food; soon a breakfast richer than the ordinary ones he was accustomed to was spread before him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After a few hours' walk he again became hungry, and went to a hut asking the old woman there if he might eat in her house, bringing his own food; Andres invited the old woman to eat with him, and she liked the food so very much that she asked to have his wonderful red cloth: 'Give me this cloth, and I will let you have my two stones in exchange. When you want to get rid of persons who annoy you, just tell these two stones where to go, and they will inflict heavy blows on the evil-doers.' Andres agreed to the exchange — but tired and exhausted, and hungry again with his red cloth gone, he sent his two stones back to their former mistress: 'Tell her that I take back my red cloth. If she refuses to give it to you, do what you think it best to do.' The stones struck the old woman with heavy blows until she fell down senseless on the floor, then rolled themselves in the red cloth and hastened back to their master with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Resuming his journey, hungry again, Andres easily gained admittance to another hut by the roadside where the witch, its only person, had just finished her dinner and had nothing left to give the starving boy. Andres spread his red cloth and ate, then asked for an extraordinary breakfast besides — and said to the witch, 'You need not prepare anything for your breakfast to-morrow. Here is a good meal that I have asked my red cloth to give to you, you have been so kind in letting me come to your hut.' The witch was very glad, and thanked the boy: 'Boy, I have here two magic canes which I want to dispose of. They can kill your enemies, or any bad persons whom you want to be put to death. Just give them directions, and they will obey you.' Andres now had three enchanted possessions. When he reached home late, his hungry and angry mother met him at the foot of the stairs with a loud scolding; but Andres just laughed, asked his red cloth to bring her a good dinner, and related the occurrences of the day while she ate. Andres and his mother were not rich, and their wealthy neighbors were greatly surprised to see them become rich so soon; one particularly selfish neighbor, eager to deprive them of their wealth, sent a band of robbers to the cottage one night. At midnight Andres heard his dogs barking; when he saw the robbers coming, he took out his magic stones and canes, and commanded them to get rid of the thieves — in a few minutes all the robbers lay dead. Andres and his mother remained rich.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 26 'An Act of Kindness'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Indolent Husband: Purse, Goat, Table, and Cane
title.zh: 懶漢丈夫：錢袋、山羊、神桌與魔杖

region.en: Tigaon, Camarines, Bicol region, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋比科爾地區蒂高安（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Bicol oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband', eBook #8299

summary.en: Whipped and kicked by his shrewish wife Barbara, the idle Alejo meets an old humpback who gives him a money-crying purse, then a gold-giving goat, then a self-serving table — each demonstrated to his drinking friends and each swapped for a common one while he sleeps. The fourth gift, a cane that lashes 'no princes, kings, or emperors' excepted, is used at home with the doors shut: the treacherous compadre and comadre buy back all three treasures, and Barbara learns her husband's wanderings were profitable.
summary.zh: 被悍妻芭芭拉拳腳相加的懶漢阿萊霍遇見老駝背：錢袋喊錢、山羊產金、神桌自陳佳餚——每次都在酒友面前顯靈，每次醉睡之後都被那對奸詐的乾親夫婦調包。第四件禮物是根連王侯也照打不誤的魔杖；他閉門宴客，魔杖飛舞——奸夫婦慌忙奉還三寶。芭芭拉終於明白：丈夫的遊歷其實有賺。

sensitivity.note: Bicol folktale recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (Tigaon, Camarines); archival record. Ass-Table-Stick cycle (Grimm No. 36 family); Fansler compares Caballero's 'Tio Curro el de la porra.'

passages.text: Many hundreds of years ago there lived in the isolated village of Hignaroy a poor couple who had many children to care for: Barbara, the wife, was an industrious but shrewish woman who worked all day in a factory to support her many children, while the husband, Alejo, idled away his time, either eating, or drinking, or sleeping all the time his wife was away at work. Barbara's anger grew so strong that she no longer used words to reform her husband: she would kick him as he lay lazily on his bed and would even whip him like a child. Finally the thought of leaving home came into his head, partly to get away from his wife, who was always interfering with his ease, and partly to seek his fortune.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Roaming through woods, over hills, and along river-banks where no human creature could be seen, he lay down to rest in the shade of a tree, meditating on his wretched condition, when an old humpback came upon him: 'Don't be worried, my son! Here, take this purse! It has nothing in it; but, if you need money at any time, just say these words — Sopot, ua-ua sopot! — and it will give you money.' Alejo went home in lively spirits, stopping at the house of his compadre and comadre, who entertained him well; when he took out his magic purse and pronounced the words, showers of silver coins dropped on the floor, and the covetous couple gave him glass after glass of wine until he was dead-drunk — then the wife stealthily untied the purse from Alejo's waist and put in its place one of their own. Before his own children, the purse gave nothing, and Barbara stormed at him with all the bitter words that can be imagined and drove him from the house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He wandered away again and found the old man, who gave him a goat: 'It will give you money if you ask for it. Whenever you want any money, just say these words: Canding, pag coroquinanding!' Again he passed by his friends' house and was entertained; when he fell asleep they exchanged his beast for one of their own, and again the magic failed before Barbara, who railed at her husband more than ever. A third gift followed — a table which, at the words 'Tende la mesa!', provides all kinds of delicious food and drink — and again the deceitful couple plied him with wine, exchanged his magic table for a common one, and Alejo went home to receive from his wife's hands 'what blows, what pinches, what whips' when not even a single grain of rice appeared on the table.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I pity you, indeed,' said the old man. 'Take this cane as my last gift. Be very careful in using it, for I have no other object to give you. The secret of this cane is this: if somebody has done you wrong, say to the cane, Baston, pamordon! and then it will lash that person. There are no princes, kings, or emperors that it will not punish.' This time, when he reached the village, Alejo did not pass by his friends' house but went directly home, telling his wife to call in all their friends, relatives, and neighbors for a sort of banquet; when all were gathered, he shut all the doors and even the windows, and shouted to his magic cane, 'Baston, pamordon!' — and it at once began to lash all the people in the house, throwing them into great confusion. At last Alejo's two friends, the deceitful couple, exclaimed almost in one voice, 'Compadre, please stop, and we will give you back your magic purse, goat, and table.' When Alejo heard them say this he was filled with joy, and commanded the cane to cease. That very day the magic purse, goat, and table were returned to him by his compadre and comadre, and now Barbara realized that her husband's wanderings had been profitable; the husband and wife became rich, and they lived many happy years together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 27 'The Indolent Husband'; not verbatim.

title.en: Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio: The Guitar That Makes All Dance
title.zh: 塞西利奧與埃米利奧：令眾人起舞的吉他

region.en: Santa Cruz, Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省聖克魯斯（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio', eBook #8299

summary.en: Cheated of his wages, Cecilio is twice robbed — the first robbers kill each other over the division — before an old woman lends him a beating cane and sells him a magic guitar. Playing it innocently as his master climbs through thorned bamboo, he makes Emilio dance among the spines; bought off with the hacienda money, accused, and condemned to be shot, Cecilio plays again at the scaffold until the whole firing party dances and Emilio, begging him to stop, bestows on the boy all his wealth.
summary.zh: 被剋扣工錢的塞西利奧兩度遭劫——第一對強盜為分贓自相殘殺而死——老嫗借他神杖、賣他魔吉他。他在竹刺叢邊無意撥弦，主人埃米利奧便在刺叢中跳個不停；他以莊園款項贖身，又被誣告判死刑。刑場之上，他再度撥弦，行刑隊跳作一團——埃米利奧哀求停止，並把全部家產贈予少年。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a de Leon narrator (Santa Cruz, Laguna); archival record. Fansler traces the dance-compelling fiddle family to the Middle-English 'Frere and the Boye' via Albrecht's 1599 German form.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a witty orphan whose name was Cecilio; his parents had died when he was six years old, and after that time he became a servant of Emilio, a man of wealth living in a very lonely and desolate barrio. The boy was faithful and kind-hearted, but his master was cruel: Cecilio had no wages at all, and served Emilio for four years, at the end of that time being given five hundred centavos as payment for his services. He thought he had been given too much — he was so simple-minded that he did not know he had been cheated by his master, who should have given him ten times five hundred centavos.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Cecilio put his money in a new purse and rushed out into the main road to find his companions; so very happy that before he knew it he had reached another barrio. Suddenly on his way he met two men with drawn bolos: 'Boy, your money, or your life!' Frightened, he gave up the money at once, and sat under a tree lamenting his fortune — but the two robbers were in trouble, because one of them wanted a greater share than the other; at this they began to fight, and soon both fell so severely wounded that they died before Cecilio, who had heard the noise of the struggle, could reach the place where they were disputing. Now the boy was very happy again, for he had gotten his money back — until he met another man who said roughly, 'Give me your money, or else you will die!' Cecilio gave his purse to the man and went away and wept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While he was crying over his bad luck, a very old woman came near him: 'Take this cane with you, and whenever you see him, let it loose and pronounce these words — Sigue garrote, sigue garrote, strike that fellow over there! When you want the cane to stop, all you need to say is — Stop, stop, for that is enough!' Cecilio ran to overtake the man who had robbed him: 'Give me back my money, or else you now shall die, and not I!' The man laughed at him — and the cane at once began to rain blows on the stranger's head and body; when he could no longer endure the blows he promised to return the purse, and Cecilio pardoned him: 'If you had treated me as you should have treated me and others, you would not have been harmed.' On his way back toward the old woman, Cecilio met another man who wanted to rob him — and the cane rained blows again until the man asked his pardon, and as the youth was kind-hearted he forgave him. When he reached the old woman's house, Cecilio told her that the cane had been very useful to him, for it had saved both his life and his money; then he returned the stick and thanked her very much. She now offered to sell him a guitar she had, the price of which was five hundred centavos, and Cecilio at once agreed to the exchange.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he came near his old home, Cecilio saw his master Emilio shooting at a very handsome bird on the top of a bamboo-tree; the bird fell down, and the man ran to pick it up. As Emilio was making his way through the thorny bamboo undergrowth, Cecilio sat down to wait for him and, having nothing else to do, began to play his guitar — and the master at once began to dance among the bamboo-trees, receiving many wounds because of the sharp spines. In reality the boy was playing his guitar unintentionally and did not know of its magic power, but Emilio thought that Cecilio had discovered the deceit that had been practised on him and was playing for revenge; it happened that Emilio had a purse of money with him to give to the laborers working in his hacienda, so he promised to give all this money to Cecilio if he would only stop playing — and the boy, who had by this time learned of the magic power of his guitar, stopped his music and received the money. The crafty Emilio at once hastened to the town and asked the magistrate to apprehend Cecilio, a young robber; arrested and sentenced to death the next morning, Cecilio asked permission to play his guitar once more when he was about to be shot, and was not refused it. As soon as he began to play, all began to dance, even his master, who was still sore from the previous day's exercise; finally Emilio could endure no more: he begged Cecilio to stop playing and promised to give him all his wealth, then told the soldiers to set the boy free, for it was all his own fault. Emilio kept his word, and bestowed on the boy all his wealth; when the old man died, Cecilio was the richest man in the town — he became a capitan, and was greatly honored by the inhabitants of his barrio.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 28 'Cecilio, the Servant of Emilio'; not verbatim.
